To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
epiphytic mycoherbivores and mycoparasites colonise cocoa flowers and pods independently of crop development stage, cultivar and resistance status.

the population dynamics of epiphyte mycoparasites are not affected by the genetic disease resistance of the host and that they are not affected by shading, but they are affected by surface-sterilisation.

the natural abundance of native, epiphitic mycoparasites in cocoa is independent of the cocoa cultivar and that the survival and recolonisation of applied mycoparasite inocula is independent from the shading regime.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ecology of epiparasites on the aerial parts of the plant, which are of direct relevance to the design of bioinocula for the application of mycoparasite-based biocontrol agents.
the ecology of epiphitic mycoparasites in cocoa agroforests and the implications for applied biocontrol.
the development of a sustainable, environmentally friendly disease control programme for cocoa.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the epiphytic mycobiota on cocoa pods is not affected by cultivar and disease resistance.

epiphytic mycoherbicides can be successfully applied to cocoa in the shade or in full sunlight, and that the application of a single biocontrol product is likely to be suitable for the control of both black pod and monilia pod rot on a wide range of cocoa cultivars.
epiphytic mycobiota of cocoa are highly diverse.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the population dynamics of native mycoparasite species on cocoa is determined by the abundance of the respective host and the prevailing microclimate.

the ecology of epiphyytic mycoparasitic fungi of the genera Clono-stachys and Fusarum on cocoa is complex, but the main factors influencing their abundance can be predicted from a limited number of easily measurable environmental parameters.
the ecology of epiparasitic mycoparasites can be predicted to a certain degree and is amenable to practical application.
The main takeaway from our work is that
epiphytic mycobiocontrol agents can be successfully used to control moniliasis and black pod of cocoa.
biocontrol agents should be applied at a frequency that allows for recolonisation by epiphytic mycobiota, especially in shaded cocoa orchards where this process is delayed.

the abundance and diversity of mycoparasite populations are not affected by the genetic disease resistance status of the cocoa plant and that shading of the cocoa canopy is not a factor that needs to be taken into account when designing biocontrol inoculum formulations.
